readerTitle: Why great leaders fail by doing what made them great
caseNote: 실제 연구 (CCL 탈선 연구, Kaplan & Kaiser) + 가상 사례 (레스토랑 그룹, 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 리더의 탈선은 약점이 드러나서가 아니라, 일이 바뀌었는데도 예전의 강점을 그대로 더 세게 쓰는 데서 시작된다.
misconception: 리더가 무너지는 건 능력이 부족하거나 게을러졌기 때문이다. 강점은 많이 쓸수록 좋다.

sources.text: McCall, M. W. & Lombardo, M. M. (1983). Off the Track: Why and How Successful Executives Get Derailed. Center for Creative Leadership.
Kaplan, R. E. & Kaiser, R. B. (2009). Stop Overdoing Your Strengths. Harvard Business Review.
레스토랑 그룹과 소프트웨어 회사 사례, 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: CCL 연구(McCall & Lombardo, 1983) 요약을 확인하세요: 정상까지 오른 임원과 탈선한 임원을 비교했고, 두 집단 모두 강점과 약점이 있었으며, 탈선 원인으로 대인관계 문제(둔감함, 오만), 신뢰 훼손, 과도한 관리, 직무 변화에 적응하지 못함 등이 꼽혔다는 내용. 카드에는 구체적 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
Kaplan & Kaiser(2009, HBR) 'Stop Overdoing Your Strengths'의 핵심 주장(강점의 과용이 성과를 해친다)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 게재 연월(2009년 2월로 알려짐)도 확인.
가상 수치 확인: 헤드셰프 시절 주 50시간 = 직접 조리·검수 45 + 코칭 5. 운영 총괄 시절 주 50시간 = 현장 직접 개입 35 + 코칭 3 + 기타 행정 12(차트에는 앞의 두 항목만 표시). 4개 매장 중 한 번에 1곳만 갈 수 있으므로 나머지 3곳은 대기.
'직급이 오를수록 솔직한 피드백이 줄어든다'는 문장은 일반적 관찰로만 썼습니다. 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why great leaders fail by doing what made them great
body: Maria ran the best kitchen in a small restaurant group. She tasted every sauce and checked every plate. Her kitchen had the best reviews and the lowest waste.
So the owner put her in charge of all four restaurants. Eighteen months later, three of the four head chefs had quit. Maria hadn't changed at all. That was the problem.

image.label: A chef stretched across four kitchen doors at once
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 셰프 한 명이 네 개의 주방 문 사이를 뛰어다니고, 문 너머 셰프들은 팔짱을 끼고 기다리는 모습. 실제 레스토랑 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What went wrong with Maria?
body: Sales are flat. Chefs who leave say they felt like line cooks in their own kitchens. Maria is working longer hours than ever.

options.text: She lost her edge after the promotion
options.feedback: It's the easy story, but she's working harder than ever. Calling it a drop in talent hides what actually changed: the job.

options.text: She kept doing what made her great, in a job that needed something else
options.feedback: Her habit of fixing every plate built one great kitchen. Across four, it left chefs with nothing to decide. The next card shows where her week went.

options.text: The group hired weak head chefs
options.feedback: Possible, and worth checking. But three strong-enough chefs leaving for the same reason points back to how they were led.

cards.title: Same hours. Same habits. Different job.
body: Maria's week stayed at about 50 hours. As head chef, 45 went to cooking and checking. As the leader of four kitchens, 35 still went to stepping in herself. Coaching her chefs fell from 5 hours to 3.

groups.label: As leader of four kitchens (hours per week)

cards.title: Derailment
body: **Derailment** is when a leader who was clearly succeeding stalls, gets moved aside or is let go.

In the early 1980s, researchers at the Center for Creative Leadership compared executives who reached the top with those who derailed. Both groups were talented and both had flaws. The derailed ones were often undone by problems with people and by failing to adapt when the job changed.

image.label: A train leaving the track at a bend
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 직선 구간에서는 빠르게 달리던 기차가 선로가 꺾이는 지점("New role")에서 직진해 선로를 이탈. 직선 구간 라벨은 "What got you here".

cards.title: Most flaws are strengths turned up too high.
body: Robert Kaplan and Robert Kaiser argued in a 2009 Harvard Business Review article that leaders often hurt their results by overdoing what they're good at. Each strength has a version that goes too far:
cards.callout: The higher you rise, the more people your overused strength lands on.

cards.title: The same habit flips its value as the job grows.
body: Fixing a plate is a gift in one kitchen. In four kitchens, every fix is a decision a head chef didn't get to make.

breakdown.label: Maria on the line
breakdown.detail: She catches every mistake. Quality goes up.

breakdown.label: Maria in one at a time
breakdown.detail: Three kitchens wait for her or guess.

breakdown.label: Left for head chefs
breakdown.detail: Strong chefs stop growing, then leave.

cards.softwareNote: A star engineer promoted to lead 40 people who still rewrites code in review shows the same flip. One great reviewer becomes a bottleneck, and senior engineers stop owning their work.

cards.title: Don't blame every failure on the leader.
body: Some leaders fail because the strategy, the market or the budget was wrong. Calling everything derailment can let a bad plan off the hook.
And the fix isn't to delete a strength. Maria's eye for quality is still valuable. The question is where to use it: setting standards and teaching them, not checking every plate.
Also, honest feedback usually thins out as people rise. Leaders often notice derailment last.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Priya was your best engineer. Now she leads 40 people. She reviews every major change and often rewrites it at night. Releases are slipping, and two team leads have hinted they might leave.
As CEO, what do you do?

options.text: Tell her to stop coding and reviewing entirely
options.feedback: It breaks the habit fast, but it throws away a real strength and can feel like a punishment. She may just find other ways to step in.

options.text: Name the overused strength, agree on where she still reviews, and get her team leads' feedback every month
options.feedback: She keeps her standards where they matter most and hands real decisions back to her leads. Regular feedback shows whether the habit is actually changing.

options.text: Hire a strong deputy to manage the team around her
options.feedback: It relieves the pressure for a while, but the root habit stays. Now two people are leading, and the team learns to route around both.

cards.title: What got you here can pull you off the track.
body: Leaders rarely derail from a lack of talent. They derail by turning up the strength that worked before, after the job has changed.
**Try it today:** write down your two biggest strengths. For each, write what it looks like when you overdo it. Ask one person on your team if they've seen it.
